newsitem.title: USA: Trauma sues Seagram affiliate Interscope.
newsitem.headline: Trauma sues Seagram affiliate Interscope.

text.p: Trauma Records said Tuesday it filed suit against Seagram Co Ltd's 50 percent-owned Interscope Records seeking $100 million in damages for alleged breach of contract and fraud in a deal involving the hit pop band "No Doubt."
The lawsuit also accuses Interscope, which is credited with boosting Seagram's Universal Music division, of negligent misrepresentation and termination of an agreement.
It alleges Interscope assigned No Doubt's recording contract to Trauma in 1995, when it was a relatively unknown band, but then reneged after the band became hugely popular.
Interscope and Trauma have had a distribution pact since 1994. The suit also seeks to terminate that agreement.
Interscope and Universal Music officials were unavailable.

"No Doubt", which was first signed to Interscope in the early 1990s, is not party to the suit. Trauma said Interscope assigned the "No Doubt" contract to Trauma in 1995 after the failure of No Doubt's first album.

Trauma said it spent a lot of time promoting and marketing the "Tragic Kingdom" album which became one of the biggest sellers in 1996. Interscope thereupon reneged on its agreement, denying it assigned No Doubt to Trauma, it said.
Trauma said the lawsuit notes Interscope previously acknowledged No Doubt is on Trauma Record's roster and the band is listed as part of Trauma's roster in industry publications.
The lawsuit also asserts that, by threatening to use its leverage of marketing budgets and royalty pipeline payments, Interscope is seeking to disrupt and harm Trauma's business.

Interscope is also co-owned by an heir to the Marshall Field fortune, Ted Field. Seagram's Universal Music division has moved from one of the industry's weakest labels to one of its strong players since it paid $200 million to buy a 50 percent share of Interscope over the past couple of years.
